id: When I Heard at the Close of the Day

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When I heard at the close of the day how my name had been receiv’d with plaudits in the capitol, still it was not a happy night for me that follow’d, And else when I carous’d, or when my plans were accomplish’d, still I was not happy, But the day when I rose at dawn from the bed of perfect health, refresh’d, singing, inhaling the ripe breath of autumn, When I saw the full moon in the west grow pale and disappear in the morning light, When I wander’d alone over the beach, and undressing bathed, laughing with the cool waters, and saw the sun rise, And when I thought how my dear friend my lover was on his way coming, O then I was happy, O then each breath tasted sweeter, and all that day my food nourish’d me more, and the beautiful day pass’d well, And the next came with equal joy, and with the next at evening came my friend, And that night while all was still I heard the waters roll slowly continually up the shores, I heard the hissing rustle of the liquid and sands as directed to me whispering to congratulate me, For the one I love most lay sleeping by me under the same cover in the cool night, In the stillness in the autumn moonbeams his face was inclined toward me, And his arm lay lightly around my breast – and that night I was happy.

outputs.L1:
This text is actually Walt Whitman's celebrated poem **"When I Heard at the Close of the Day"** from *Leaves of Grass*—already a polished literary masterpiece. That said, here is a refined version rendered in more formal, flowing prose while preserving all the original meaning:

---

When word reached me at the close of day that my name had been received with acclaim in the Capitol, the night that followed brought me no happiness. Nor did I find contentment in revelry, nor even in the fulfillment of my ambitions.

Yet true joy came upon the day I rose at dawn in perfect health—refreshed, singing, drawing in the ripe breath of autumn. It came as I watched the full moon fade in the western sky and vanish into the morning light. It came as I wandered alone along the shore, cast off my garments, bathed in laughter amid the cool waters, and beheld the rising sun. And it came when I reflected that my dear friend, my beloved, was even then journeying toward me.

Oh, in that moment I was happy! Each breath tasted the sweeter; all that day my nourishment sustained me more fully, and the beautiful hours passed serenely. The next day dawned with equal gladness, and by the evening that followed, my beloved arrived.

That night, while all lay still, I heard the waters roll ceaselessly and slowly upon the shores; I heard the soft, hissing murmur of water and sand, as though whispering to me in congratulation. For the one I love most lay sleeping beside me beneath the same blanket in the cool night. In the quiet, bathed in autumn moonbeams, his face was turned toward mine, and his arm rested lightly across my breast—and that night, I was happy.

---

outputs.L2:
As the day drew to an end, word reached me that my name had been celebrated with applause in the capitol—yet the evening that followed brought me no true joy. On other occasions too, whether I was feasting merrily or watching my ambitions come to fruition, contentment still eluded me.

But there was a morning when I woke at daybreak, my body in flawless health, feeling renewed, humming a tune, and breathing in the rich, mature air of autumn. I watched the full moon in the western sky fade and vanish as the morning brightness spread. I strolled by myself along the shoreline, shed my clothes, and swam, delighting in the chill of the water while I witnessed the sunrise. And as I reflected on the fact that my beloved companion was traveling toward me—oh, in that moment I felt genuine happiness.

Then every breath I drew seemed sweeter, my meals gave me greater nourishment throughout the day, and that lovely day unfolded beautifully. The following day arrived bringing the same delight, and when evening fell on the day after that, my friend finally reached me.

That night, amid the complete quiet, I listened to the waters lapping steadily and endlessly against the shore. I heard the soft, whispering hiss of the water meeting the sand, and it seemed to speak to me alone, as if offering its congratulations. For the person I cherish above all was lying asleep beside me, sharing the same blanket in the cool of the night. In that hush, beneath the autumn moonlight, his face turned gently toward mine, and his arm rested softly across my chest—and on that night, I knew happiness.

# On the True Sources of Happiness

Throughout his life, the speaker had pursued many of the things that society holds up as markers of success. Yet in reflecting upon them, he confesses a surprising truth: public recognition, the applause of crowds, and the personal achievements he had accumulated brought him no lasting happiness or genuine contentment. The honors and celebrations that others might envy left him strangely empty, unable to satisfy the deeper longings of his heart.

Instead, he discovered that true joy arose from the simplest of experiences—those quiet moments offered freely by the natural world. To wake at dawn in perfect health, to feel his body refreshed and whole, brought him a happiness that no accolade could match. Bathing in cool, clear waters and watching the sun break slowly over the horizon filled him with a contentment more profound than any triumph the world could offer.

This happiness grew richer still with the anticipation of his beloved friend's arrival. The mere expectation of that reunion cast a warm glow over everything around him. Even the food he ate seemed to taste sweeter, and the beauty of the day appeared heightened, as though his inner joy had transformed the world into something more vivid and alive.

When his friend at last arrived, the speaker's happiness seemed to overflow into the landscape itself. He felt that all of nature had become a partner in his gladness—the very waters, rolling and murmuring in the distance, appeared to whisper their congratulations, as if the world rejoiced alongside him.

Yet the deepest and most treasured happiness of all came in the stillness of the night. To lie in intimate closeness beside the one he loved most, sharing the peace and quiet of an autumn evening, was for the speaker the very height of contentment. In that tender nearness, undisturbed and complete, he found the fulfillment that all the honors and achievements of the world had never been able to give him.
outputs.L4:
# On True Happiness

There was a time when I believed that happiness could be measured—counted in the applause of crowds, weighed in the medals pinned to my chest, catalogued in the newspaper columns that spoke my name to strangers. I chased these markers of success as a runner chases the horizon, always certain that fulfillment waited just beyond the next achievement, the next honor, the next public recognition of my worth.

The world had taught me well. It handed me its trophies and its titles, and for a season I mistook their glitter for gold. I stood before admiring faces and felt myself grow large in their estimation. Surely, I thought, this is what it means to have arrived. Surely this swelling of pride, this satisfaction of ambition realized, is the happiness that poets praise and philosophers pursue.

Yet in the quiet hours, when the crowds dispersed and the noise of acclaim faded into silence, I felt the emptiness that fame leaves in its wake—a hollowness that no accolade could fill.

It was then that I began to notice smaller things. The way morning light spills golden across a dew-wet field. The song of a single bird, unconcerned with audiences or applause. The gentle murmur of a stream that has never sought a single word of praise for its endless, patient flowing. Here, in these unremarkable moments, I found a peace that all my triumphs had never granted me.

And there was something more—someone more.

Beside me now, in the tender hush of early morning, sleeps a beloved friend. I watch the slow rise and fall of quiet breathing, the untroubled face at rest, and I understand at last what all my striving failed to teach me. This—this simple presence, this intimate trust, this love that asks for nothing and gives everything—*this* is the treasure I spent so long overlooking.

For what is fame but the opinion of those who do not truly know us? And what is success but a fleeting shadow that vanishes when the sun of public interest moves on? These things cannot warm us in the night. They cannot hold our hand in sorrow or share our laughter in joy. They are echoes, not embraces.

But nature endures, offering its quiet gifts to any heart willing to receive them. And love endures, deeper than any honor the world can bestow. In the company of the natural world and in the presence of one who loves me, I have discovered the happiness that eluded me for so long.

I needed no external voice to validate my worth. I needed only to be still, to be present, to be here—beneath the open sky, beside a sleeping friend, alive to the simple miracles that surround us all.

This, I now know, is true happiness: not the roar of the crowd, but the whisper of the wind through leaves; not the weight of medals, but the warmth of a hand in mine; not the fleeting praise of many, but the abiding love of one. In quiet moments such as these, I have found everything I ever truly sought.

# When, And, But: The Small Words That Shape Our Language

Some of the most powerful words in the English language are also among the shortest. Words like *when*, *and*, and *but* may seem simple, yet they carry enormous weight in how we communicate, connect ideas, and express our thoughts.

## When

The word *when* is all about time and conditions. It helps us organize our experiences and understand the sequence of events. **When** we wake up in the morning, we begin a new day. **When** it rains, we reach for an umbrella. This little word invites us to consider timing, cause, and circumstance. It can turn a simple statement into a story: "Call me **when** you arrive" suggests anticipation and connection across time.

## And

If any word represents connection, it is *and*. This tiny conjunction links our thoughts, joins our ideas, and builds bridges between separate elements. We use it to add, to accumulate, and to continue. Without *and*, our sentences would be short, fragmented, and disconnected. It allows us to say more, to combine experiences, and to show that life is rarely about single things standing alone.

## But

Then comes *but*—the word of contrast and surprise. Where *and* joins, *but* introduces tension and change. It signals that something unexpected is coming. "I wanted to go outside, **but** it was raining." This word acknowledges complexity, showing that life is full of contradictions and exceptions. *But* keeps us honest, reminding us that not everything fits neatly together.

## Conclusion

Together, *when*, *and*, and *but* demonstrate how much meaning can live in the smallest words. They shape our sentences, guide our logic, and reflect the way we think about time, connection, and contrast. Small in size **but** mighty in purpose, these words prove that language does not need to be complicated to be powerful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Walt Whitman poem about how quiet personal happiness matters more than public praise or accomplishment.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Quiet Yield**

O I have seen the great processions, the banners and the shouting crowds,
The names carved deep in marble, the applause that swells and dies away,
And I have stood among the honored, the medals cold upon my breast—
Yet I tell you, comrade, listen close: these are not the sum of a life.

Give me instead the early morning, the light unhurried on the sill,
The warm cup held in both my hands, the steam that rises and is gone,
The unremarkable bread, the plain table, the window open to the wren—
These, these are the true republic of a man's contentment!

What is the roar of the multitude to the low laugh of one I love?
What is the statue in the square to the print of a bare foot on the floor?
I have tasted fame, that thin broth, and risen still hungry from the table;
I have known one quiet afternoon, and been fed for a hundred years.

You who chase the loud reward, who lie awake counting the eyes upon you—
Come, lie here in the ordinary grass, where no one keeps the score,
Where the ant goes about its errand and the cloud asks nothing of you,
Where being is enough, and to breathe is the whole and sufficient wage.

I sing the unwitnessed happiness! I sing the joy no ledger holds!
The tenderness given in darkness, the kindness that seeks no credit,
The small unfinished tasks, the mending, the tending, the near-at-hand—
For the soul is not enlarged by monuments, but by the loving of little things.

Let others have the pedestal, the headline, the fading crown of the hour.
I will take the hand beside me, the supper, the shared and settling dusk,
And when at last I go, unnoticed, into the grass I have praised,
Know that I was rich, O comrade—I was quietly, wholly, immeasurably rich.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free verse poem in the style of Leaves of Grass describing a night spent beside a beloved friend by the sea.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nocturne by the Salt-Wide Water

Come, let me sing of the night we lay beside the sea,
You and I, two forms upon the cooling sand,
The great dark water breathing, breathing, an old animal at rest,
And I breathing with it, and you breathing with me.

O the largeness of that dark! I say it plainly—
The stars were not distant but leaned close as lovers,
The whole sky an intimate multitude,
And we two small and unashamed beneath it.

I heard the waves come in and go out,
Come in and go out, tireless, saying nothing and saying all,
And I thought: this is the pulse of the world,
This the same tide that laves the coast of every longing man.

You did not speak, and I did not need your speaking.
Your shoulder against my shoulder was a whole language,
Your breath the punctuation of a poem older than words.
I tell you the touch of a friend is a democracy of the flesh—
It asks no title, it grants no rank, it simply is.

I looked at you sleeping and loved the animal of you,
The salt in your hair, the warmth coming off your skin,
The rise and fall of your chest like a small ship at anchor.
I loved you not for what you gave but for your being,
For the sheer fact of you here, particular, unrepeatable,
One companion out of all the teeming continents.

And I thought of the dead who once lay so by the sea,
And the living who lie so tonight in a thousand thousand places,
And the ones not yet born who will lie so when we are dust—
And I felt myself a thread in that endless fabric,
Neither first nor last, but present, present, gloriously present.

The moon laid down its silver road upon the water,
A road no foot has walked and every soul has traveled.
I did not wake you. I let you rest.
I kept the vigil of gladness for us both.

When the gray dawn came fingering the horizon,
I was not sorry, for the day is good as the night is good,
And you stirred, and opened your eyes, and knew me,
And that knowing was worth more than any sunrise—

Though the sunrise, too, was worth the whole wide world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 19th-century style poem contrasting fame and applause with the simple joy of nature, bathing at dawn, and being with the one you love.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Truer Splendor

What is the roar of crowded halls,
The trumpet's brazen, boasting sound,
The laurel wreath, the marble walls,
Where hollow praise doth echo round?

Let others chase the fickle fame
That fades as quick as morning dew,
And carve in stone a fleeting name—
I seek a joy more pure, more true.

At dawn I rise while shadows flee,
And to the silver river go,
Where willows bend their boughs to me
And cooling waters gently flow.

I plunge beneath the waking stream,
The sun a coral crown above;
No richer king could ever dream
Of wealth like this—the peace I love.

The blackbird pipes his liquid song,
No sweeter than my lover's voice,
Who waits upon the bank so long,
And makes my beating heart rejoice.

Her hand in mine, the meadows wide,
The dew that jewels every blade—
What need have I for pomp and pride,
For crowns that rust and glories fade?

So let the world its plaudits keep,
Its gilded thrones, its restless fame;
Give me the dawn, the river deep,
And love that whispers low my name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
